pages.name: A warm-up
pages.task: A float rides in fresh water. You move it to seawater, which is denser. What does the float do?
pages.why: A float sinks until the liquid it pushes aside weighs as much as the float. Seawater is denser, so a smaller volume of it weighs enough. The float needs to push aside less, so it rides higher. A hydrometer uses the same idea to weigh battery acid.

pages.name: Two gauges
pages.text: Here is the lead-acid cell again, with two gauges on it. The [[hydrometer]] holds a sample of its acid around a float. Its scale reads [[specific gravity]], the acid's density divided by water's. Denser liquid holds a float higher. The voltmeter reads the cell's voltage. As the cell charges, acid leaves the plates for the liquid. So the float rises. Stronger acid makes the cell rest a little higher, so the voltmeter climbs too. At 90% charge they read 1.213 and 2.06 V.

pages.name: Running down
pages.task: The cell starts full and discharges to half. What does the float do?
pages.answer: It sinks lower as the acid thins
pages.why: Discharge locks acid into the lead sulphate on the plates. The liquid left is lighter and more like water. Lighter liquid holds the float less, so it sinks. At half charge it reads 1.165.

pages.name: Warm acid
pages.text: Temperature moves the float too. Warm acid expands, so it is less dense and reads low. Cold acid reads high. Makers correct it to a set temperature, here 25 °C. The scale counts in [[points]], and one point is 0.001. One rule adds a point for every 1.67 °C above 25 °C. Below 25 °C it takes points off the same way. At 40 °C this full cell reads 1.216, but the corrected reading holds at 1.225. The checks below fill in as you go.

pages.task: The float reads 1.219 with the acid at 35 °C. What is the corrected reading?
pages.why: 35 °C is 10 °C above 25 °C. So the correction is 10 ÷ 1.67, about 6 points. Warm acid reads low, so add them. 1.219 + 0.006 = 1.225, which is full.

pages.name: Rest it first
pages.text: The voltmeter can be fooled too. Straight after a charge it reads high. That is [[surface charge]]. One way to picture it is fresh acid left right at the plates, which takes hours to spread. This cell has just come off charge at 2.20 V. As it rests, the reading falls to 2.07 V, its rested value. So rest a cell on open circuit for at least four hours before you trust its voltage. Makers recommend 24.

pages.name: Just off charge
pages.task: A cell reads 2.20 V ten minutes after a charge. What does that tell you?
pages.answer: Not much yet, so rest it or briefly discharge it
pages.why: Straight after a charge, the voltage sits high for hours. That is surface charge. One way to picture it is fresh acid still at the plates, waiting to spread. So 2.20 V says little yet. Rest the cell for at least four hours, or give it a brief discharge. Then read it.

pages.name: The level
pages.text: The level matters too. Water evaporates, but the acid stays behind. So a low cell holds stronger acid, and its float reads high. An overfilled cell reads low. Here the level has fallen below its mark. The full cell's float now reads 1.235, above its full mark. Top up with distilled water, never acid, because only water has gone. Let it mix before you read again.

pages.name: Topping up
pages.task: A cell's level has fallen by evaporation. What should you top it up with?
pages.why: Only water evaporates. The acid stays, so the liquid left is too strong and reads high. Distilled water brings it back to strength. Let it mix, and the float reads 1.225 again.

pages.name: Layers
pages.text: Acid can also settle into layers, with strong acid at the bottom. That is [[stratification]]. The lower parts of the plates then stand in strong acid, which lifts their voltage. So the voltmeter reads high, and the cell looks more charged than it is. This cell is at 90%, yet its voltmeter reads 2.11 V. The hydrometer gives no single reading, because that depends on where its sample comes from. The mixed check fails, so the light says not yet.

pages.name: Reads well, runs short
pages.task: This cell has rested a day and its level is right. Its voltmeter reads high, yet it runs out early. What makes it read high?
pages.why: The acid has settled into layers, with strong acid at the bottom. The lower parts of the plates stand in it, which lifts the voltage. So the cell looks more charged than it is, and it runs out early.

pages.name: Cold acid
pages.task: The float reads 1.228 with the acid at 20 °C. What is the corrected reading?
pages.why: 20 °C is 5 °C below 25 °C. So the correction is 5 ÷ 1.67, about 3 points. Cold acid reads high, so take them off. 1.228 − 0.003 = 1.225, which is full.

pages.name: Which to trust
pages.task: Which of these three readings can you trust?
pages.answer: 2.06 V, rested a day, level right, acid mixed
pages.why: The first cell has rested a day, its level is right and its acid is mixed. So its 2.06 V can be trusted. For this cell, that is about 90% charge. The second still carries surface charge. The third reads high because its level is low.
